title: Selective suppression of harmful cyanobacteria in an entire lake with hydrogen peroxide
scale: lab incubations; duplicate lake enclosures (0, 2.5, 5, 8 mg/L); whole Lake Koetshuis, NL (~0.12 km2, max depth 2 m) with untreated Lake Langebosch as reference
dose: 2.0 mg/L H2O2 target (23 mL of 10% stock per m3 via water harrow), once; measured 1.0-2.5 mg/L within 3 h
result: Cyanobacteria fell from 600x10^3 cells/mL the day before to <10x10^3 cells/mL within 10 days (microcystin followed with a 2-day lag) while the untreated reference lake kept rising; numbers stayed low for 7 weeks, then rose to ~200x10^3 cells/mL by end of September. In enclosures, P. agardhii was >98% below control at day 9.
env_effects: H2O2 fell to 0.7 mg/L after 1 day and below detection after 2 days. Enclosures: zooplankton (Daphnia, Diaphanosoma) fell ~35% at 2.5 mg/L and nearly vanished at 5-8 mg/L; green algae showed cell-wall damage at 5-8 mg/L. Whole lake at 2 mg/L: zooplankton stable for 5 weeks, eukaryotic phytoplankton not strongly affected, ammonium spiked after lysis, and transparency did not improve (stayed 45-60 cm).
key_details: Stepwise design: lab incubations (duplicates) showed 1-4 mg/L cut photosynthetic vitality to <30% within 3 h, with ~0.3 mg/L consumed by water-matrix reactions; duplicate lake enclosures at 2.5, 5 and 8 mg/L cut P. agardhii >98% vs control by day 9 but higher doses nearly eliminated zooplankton, so 2 mg/L was chosen for the whole lake. Whole-lake treatment (single lake, unreplicated, one untreated reference lake) collapsed the Planktothrix bloom within 10 days and microcystin followed. Recovery began after ~7 weeks with P. agardhii plus invading Woronichinia naegeliana. Water clarity did not improve despite the collapse.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's '99% within a few days' is slightly compressed: counts fell from 600x10^3 to <10x10^3 cells/mL within 10 days. Record omitted that enclosure doses >=5 mg/L nearly eliminated zooplankton (and 2.5 mg/L cut it ~35%), that transparency did not improve, and that cyanobacteria returned after 7 weeks. Whole-lake part is n=1 with one reference lake.

title: Termination of a toxic Alexandrium bloom with hydrogen peroxide
scale: whole brackish creek (after lab and canal tests)
result: Vegetative cells and pellicle cysts -99.8% within 48 h; PSP toxins below 15 µg/L; bloom recurred at lower levels the next year.
env_effects: Zooplankton strongly affected; macroinvertebrates and fish minimally.

title: Applicability of Hydrogen Peroxide in Brown Tide Control – Culture and Microcosm Studies
organism: Aureococcus anophagefferens + 11 marine species (Phaeodactylum, T. pseudonana, T. weissflogii, P. micans, Amphidinium, Micromonas, etc.)
scale: cultures + Barnegat Bay seawater microcosms
result: 1.6 mg/L cut Aureococcus chl-a >90% by 24 h (24-h EC50 0.91 mg/L); of the other 11 species only Micromonas was eradicated; at 6.4 mg/L P. micans (11.2%) and T. weissflogii (2.6%) were not significantly inhibited; inhibition fell with cell size.
env_effects: Microcosms: diatoms and greens dipped, then exceeded controls within 72 h; cyanobacteria down about 50%.

title: Effect of algal growth phase on Aureococcus anophagefferens susceptibility to hydrogen peroxide
scale: cultures at 1.6×10⁶ cells/mL
result: Stationary-phase cells had weaker ROS scavenging and needed 30-40% less H2O2 for 90% removal within 12 h.
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Mitigation of Marine Dinoflagellates Using Hydrogen Peroxide (H2O2) Increases Toxicity towards Epithelial Gill Cells
organism: Alexandrium catenella, Karenia selliformis, Lepidodinium, Prorocentrum micans; RTgill-W1 fish gill cells
scale: cultures at 1000 cells/mL (salinity 25/33) + gill-cell assay
result: 50 mg/L (lowest dose tested) killed all 4 dinoflagellates, leaving photosynthetic efficiency at 12% and viability at 6.4%; gill-cell toxicity rose, even with non-toxic P. micans and Lepidodinium.
env_effects: Lysed cells made the water more toxic to fish gill cells (aldehydes from lipid peroxidation proposed); H2O2 alone cytotoxic to gill cells, fading after 24 h below 200 ppm.

title: Removal of the red tide dinoflagellate Cochlodinium polykrikoides using chemical disinfectants
scale: 10 mL batch reactors (25 mL flasks), 22 +/- 2 C; C. polykrikoides 0.5-3x10^3 cells/mL; fish 72 h acute tests
dose: H2O2 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 mg/L (O3 0.5-5; MnO4- and NaOCl 0.1-5 mg/L)
duration: minutes to 3 h (cell removal); 72 h (fish LC50)
result: All four oxidants inactivated and lysed C. polykrikoides with efficacy O3 > MnO4- > NaOCl > H2O2; 10 mg/L H2O2 completely inactivated 3x10^3 cells/mL in 3 h. Fish 72-h LC50s were 1.35 (O3, estimated), 0.39 (MnO4-), 1.32 (NaOCl) and 102.61 mg/L (H2O2).
env_effects: O3 and NaOCl formed bromate (probable human carcinogen) via HOBr; MnO4- and H2O2 formed no detectable bromate or significant residual oxidants. Red sea bream showed no mortality at 50 mg/L H2O2 over 72 h; low H2O2 fish toxicity was also confirmed in juvenile starry flounder. Authors judge H2O2 the most practical and safe option.
key_details: Lab batch comparison of four disinfectants against cultured C. polykrikoides at several doses and initial cell densities, with triplicate sampling at each time point and sulfite quenching. Removal rates fell with higher cell density for all oxidants, but less so for H2O2 because its decay was little affected by cells. H2O2 needed higher doses (up to 10 mg/L) to match the others. Fish acute toxicity (probit LC50) showed H2O2 ~75-260x safer than the other oxidants.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record said the effective H2O2 dose was not in the abstract; full text shows complete inactivation of 3x10^3 cells/mL at 10 mg/L in 3 h, with doses tested 0.1-10 mg/L.

title: Treatment of the red tide dinoflagellate Karenia brevis and brevetoxins using USEPA-registered algaecides
scale: lab, natural bloom density (1.79×10⁷ cells/L)
result: K. brevis needed 4.89-7.08 mg/L of the peroxide products vs 0.31-0.34 mg Cu/L for copper; the most stable product lost 0.467 mg/L per day in natural seawater.
env_effects: Decay faster with salinity, microbes and particles ≥0.2 µm; authors call for pilot studies on marine non-targets.

title: Evaluation of algaecide effectiveness of five different oxidants applied on harmful phytoplankton
scale: lab; 100 mL subcultures in natural Cadiz Bay seawater + f/2, started at ~10^4 cells/mL (ballast-water context)
dose: dose-response per oxidant; H2O2 EC50 6.67-7.08 mg/L
result: H2O2 gave a moderate growth inhibition sustained over 14 d with similar effect on both species (EC50 6.67-7.08 mg/L); PMS and PAA were stronger but depleted within 24 h, and PDS failed to inhibit growth.
env_effects: H2O2 half-life in the cultures 0.2-0.3 days at 7.5 mg/L.
key_details: Cultured Prymnesium parvum and Heterosigma akashiwo (Spanish isolates) were grown to ~10^4 cells/mL and split into 100 mL subcultures dosed with H2O2, peracetic acid, peroxymonosulfate, peroxydisulfate or hypochlorite, with untreated negative controls. Cell density was tracked by calibrated fluorescence every 2 days and oxidant decay daily for 14 d; EC50s came from integrated growth curves. H2O2 EC50 was 6.67-7.08 mg/L with a sustained effect and similar potency on both species; PMS (EC50 0.40-1.99 mg/L) and PAA (0.32-2.70 mg/L) were stronger but short-lived; PDS had negligible effect. The authors warn that concentration-response readings before day 7 can mislead. Replicate numbers were not stated in the text read.

title: Chemical Control of Ichthyotoxic Algal Blooms in Aquaculture: Assessing Algicide Impacts on Cellular Motility and Bloom Suppression
organism: Prymnesium parvum, Heterosigma akashiwo, Fibrocapsa japonica
scale: cultures (f/2, f/20)
result: 24-h EC50: 3.35 (P. parvum), 6.01 (H. akashiwo), 7.86 (F. japonica) mg/L; motility and mean squared displacement fell at sublethal doses.
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Combating Toxic Blooms of Prymnesium parvum: Hydrogen Peroxide Influence on the Haptophyte, Other Phytoplankton Taxa, and Concentrations of Prymnesins Under Experimental Conditions
scale: four 40 L tanks of Gliwice Canal bloom water (one control + one tank per dose, no replication), continuous light
duration: 12 d stage 1 + 15 d stage 2 (after 15 L re-inoculation with bloom water)
result: P. parvum fell 98.6%, 98.8% and 99.0% within 24 h at 14, 28 and 42 mg/L, with no living cells by day 3 and no recovery through day 12; after re-inoculation with bloom water P. parvum in the 14 and 28 mg/L tanks rose above the control.
env_effects: Total phytoplankton biomass dropped 83%, 84% and 81% in 24 h; filamentous cyanobacteria (Planktothrix agardhii, Pseudanabaena limnetica) disappeared, green algae then dominated (~80% in T1). H2O2 was below 1 mg/L by day 3. Prymnesins decomposed rather than being released abruptly; a shift toward PRM 990 and higher per-cell toxin after re-inoculation.
key_details: Water from a P. parvum bloom in the Gliwice Canal (Poland, April 2023) was split into four 40 L tanks: a control and single doses of 14, 28 and 42 mg/L H2O2; each treatment is a single unreplicated tank. P. parvum declined 98.6-99.0% within 24 h and no living cells remained by day 3 in any treated tank; total phytoplankton biomass fell 81-84% in 24 h. H2O2 dropped to about 3, <10 and 30 mg/L after 24 h and was undetectable after day 3. On day 12, 15 L of each tank was replaced with fresh bloom water (4.6 x 10^7 cells/L): P. parvum in T1 and T2 then exceeded the control, while T3 tracked the control. Prymnesins were degraded along with the cells, but the regrown population had a more toxic profile.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's duration was 'Not reported'; the lab setting was actually 40 L tanks of natural canal bloom water with no replication, and the 14 mg/L dose already gave 98.6% kill in 24 h.

title: An effective algaecide for the targeted destruction of Karenia brevis
scale: lab; 500 mL K. brevis cultures (~26,000 cells/mL) and 30 mL settling columns with PAC + CaO2 (~4,500 cells/mL)
dose: CaO2 10, 30, 50 mg/L (30 mg/L releases about 8 mg/L H2O2; 10 mg/L about 2.8 mg/L), with polyaluminum chloride
duration: 72 h (cells lysed within 3 h at 50 mg/L)
result: 30 and 50 mg/L CaO2 killed K. brevis with no recovery, and with PAC removed >98% of cells from the water column in 72 h vs control; 10 mg/L gave ~80% removal at 24 h followed by partial recovery.
env_effects: CaO2 alone cut PbTx-2 by 90% and PbTx-3 by 80% at 24 h vs control; PAC alone did not degrade toxins, and PAC+CaO2 degraded them less than CaO2 alone. Off-target effects were not tested.
key_details: Lab study with cultured K. brevis (CCMP 2281 at Tulane; CCMP 2228 at Mote). CaO2 converted about 82% to H2O2 in seawater. In 500 mL cultures, 10 mg/L CaO2 cut cells at first but they recovered by 48 h while the control grew 81%; 30 and 50 mg/L caused lasting loss of viability and falling Fv/Fm. Combined with PAC flocculation in 30 mL columns, 30-50 mg/L removed >98% of cells vs control in 72 h, while PAC alone removed 76% in 24 h but the column was repopulated by 72 h. Toxin data are described by the authors as preliminary; replication was not clearly stated in the text read, and no non-target organisms were tested despite the 'minimal off-target impact' claim.
fulltext_discrepancy: Abstract-based record gave no removal percentage or toxin numbers; the 10 mg/L dose failed (recovery by 48 h), and the 'targeted, minimal off-target' claim is untested.

title: Hydrogen peroxide lifetimes in south Florida coastal and offshore waters
scale: South Florida coastal and offshore water
result: First-order decay of natural H2O2; half-life <10 h in coastal water, >120 h open ocean; decay mostly biological (organisms <1 µm).
env_effects: n/a (fate study).

title: The effects of hydrogen peroxide on mortality, escape response, and oxygen consumption of Calanus spp.
scale: lab, 1 h pulses
dose: 8.5, 17, 85, 170 mg/L H2O2 (plus 340 and 1700 mg/L in a preliminary test); 1h-LC50 214.1 (CV) / 48.3 adult in Table 2 (48.6 in abstract); 25h-LC50 77.1 / 30.6 mg/L; 25h-LC10 10.9 (CV) / 11.6 (adult) mg/L
result: Total mortality after a 1 h pulse + 24 h recovery was 30% (CV) and 14% (adults) at 17 mg/L, 34% and 89% at 85 mg/L, and 92% and 100% at 170 mg/L; none at 8.5 mg/L, but escape performance was already impaired at 8.5 and 17 mg/L and absent at 85 mg/L.
env_effects: Non-target harm; authors warn 'safe' values underestimate harm.
key_details: Wild Calanus spp. (copepodite V and adult females) from Austevoll, Norway were given 1 h H2O2 exposures then 24 h recovery; the mortality test was run in triplicate (Table 1 N = 324 copepodite V and 327 adults), with no control mortality. Mortality rose steeply with dose: 0% at 8.5 mg/L, 14-30% at 17 mg/L, up to 100% at 170 mg/L. The 25h-LC10 was about 11 mg/L for both stages, i.e. within the 14 mg/L-plus range used on HABs. Escape distance fell 1.4 mm per 10 mg/L and oxygen consumption fell with dose. Context is salmon-lice treatment (1700 mg/L), so the doses and pulse design are not a HAB treatment.
fulltext_discrepancy: Adult 1h-LC50 is 48.3 in the paper's Table 2 but 48.6 in the abstract (the record used 48.6). The 25h-LC10 of ~11 mg/L is the more relevant non-target threshold for HAB dosing.

title: Gill damage and delayed mortality of Northern shrimp (Pandalus borealis) after short time exposure to anti-parasitic veterinary medicine containing hydrogen peroxide
scale: lab flow-through tanks, 6.8 C; Exp 1-2: 6 replicate tanks x 10 shrimp per treatment; Exp 3: 4 tanks x 6 shrimp
duration: 1-2 h pulses (once, or on 3 consecutive days); 2-12 d recovery
result: Three 2 h pulses of 15 mg/L killed 46% after the third pulse and 80% two days later; three pulses of 1.5 mg/L killed 33%; a single 2 h pulse of 15 mg/L killed 50% with deaths starting on day 3; 0.15 mg/L caused no deaths.
env_effects: Gill swelling, haemocyte infiltration, fusion and necrosis after a single 1 h pulse of 1.5 or 15 mg/L; feeding 66% below control 12 days after three 1.5 mg/L pulses.
key_details: Female Northern shrimp in a continuous-flow seawater system were given PARAMOVE (H2O2 anti-sea-lice product) pulses with clean-water recovery. Exp 1-2 used 6 replicate tanks of 10 shrimp; Exp 3 used 4 tanks of 6 shrimp; no control mortality in any experiment. Mortality was delayed: none immediately after pulses, then 80% for 3 x 15 mg/L, 33% for 3 x 1.5 mg/L and 50% for one 2 h 15 mg/L pulse (one-pulse differences at lower doses not significant). Gills were progressively damaged at 1.5 and 15 mg/L, and feeding stayed depressed through 12 d of recovery. Delayed effects mean short-term toxicity tests underestimate harm.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record omitted the 80% mortality after three 15 mg/L pulses and the sublethal effects (gill necrosis, feeding -66%) at 1.5 mg/L, a dose far below HAB treatment doses.

title: The Acute and Delayed Mortality of the Northern Krill (Meganyctiphanes norvegica) When Exposed to Hydrogen Peroxide
venue: Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology
scale: lab, 1 h exposure
dose: 1.7, 8.5, 17, 170, 850 and 1700 mg/L H2O2 for 1 h (0.1-100% of the 1700 mg/L salmon-delousing dose)
duration: 1 h exposure, then 48 h post-exposure in clean seawater (checks at 6, 24, 48 h)
result: 1 h at 170 mg/L killed 100% of krill; acute 1h-LC50 32.5 mg/L (16.8-48.2), falling to 14.11 mg/L at 6 h, 4.92 mg/L at 24 h and 0.86 mg/L at 48 h post-exposure.
env_effects: Non-target delayed mortality; 48 h post-exposure LC50 0.86 mg/L after only a 1 h pulse. No mortality at 1.7 mg/L or in controls. Authors call krill the most sensitive species tested so far.
key_details: Wild Meganyctiphanes norvegica caught by light trap in Norway, exposed for 1 h to six H2O2 concentrations in 500 mL glassware at 8 C, then moved to clean seawater. 140 krill: 7 groups (incl. control) x 4 replicates x 5 krill. LC50s from probit GLM. Acute 1h-LC50 32.5 mg/L; delayed LC50 fell to 0.86 mg/L at 48 h. Context is salmon-lice bath treatment (1500-2100 mg/L), not HAB treatment, but the 48 h LC50 is below common HAB H2O2 doses.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record gave only the acute LC50; the delayed 48 h LC50 (0.86 mg/L) is ~38x lower and is the key number.

title: Acute Toxicological Response of Daphnia and Moina to Hydrogen Peroxide
organism: Daphnia carinata (s.l.) and Moina sp. clonal cultures, Western Australia (non-target zooplankton)
scale: lab acute tests in 1.2 um filtered lake water with food, 21 C, n=3 per concentration
dose: Moina 14 concentrations 0-12,500 mg/L; Daphnia 16 concentrations 0-12,500 mg/L
result: 48-h LC50 (probit) 5.6 mg/L for Daphnia (95% CI 5-6.3) and 2 mg/L for Moina (linear regression 5.7 and 1.9); NOAEC 3 and 1.5 mg/L. Complete mortality at >=3 mg/L for Moina and >=12.5 mg/L for Daphnia within 48 h.
env_effects: Non-target lethal levels near cyanobacterial treatment doses.
key_details: Acute 48 h exposures of 20 adults per species acclimated in filtered lake water, fed Desmodesmus, under low light to limit H2O2 breakdown, with three replicates per concentration; survival checked 10 times over 48 h. Moina reached 100% mortality within 12 h at >=6 mg/L; Daphnia needed >40 mg/L for 100% mortality within 12 h. Mean survival time was significantly longer in Daphnia at >=2 mg/L (Kaplan-Meier). Moina's NOAEC-LC50 gap is very small, so any effect already means high mortality. Context is waste stabilisation ponds; food was added, which may alter toxicity compared with standard tests.
fulltext_discrepancy: Minor: Moina LC50 is 2 mg/L (probit) / 1.9 mg/L (regression). Complete Moina mortality occurred at doses as low as 3 mg/L, within the range used for cyanobacteria treatment.

title: The Effects of Sodium Percarbonate Generated Free Oxygen on Daphnia—Implications for the Management of Harmful Algal Blooms
organism: Daphnia in a natural plankton sample (non-target)
scale: lab microcosms: ten 1 L containers of lake water (3 controls, one container per SP dose), 1944 zooplankton counted (1610 Daphnia)
result: Daphnia survival was 97.9% in controls, fell slightly at 5-10 mg/L SP, dropped ~50 percentage points between 20 and 30 mg/L SP (5.5-8.3 mg/L H2O2), was 3% at 40 mg/L SP (11.1 mg/L H2O2), 1.1% at 50 and 0% at 60 mg/L SP (16.6 mg/L H2O2).
env_effects: Non-target harm above the safe level.
key_details: Surface water from a shallow Polish lake (phytoplankton dominated by cryptophytes and chlorophytes; cyanobacteria ~3%) was split into ten 1 L containers: three controls and single, unreplicated containers at 5-60 mg/L sodium percarbonate. Survival was counted after 24 h; percarbonate concentration and Daphnia survival were strongly inversely correlated (Spearman r = -0.976). The authors recommend keeping doses below 10 mg/L SP (2.8 mg/L H2O2) to protect zooplankton. Algal effects were not measured, and the design has no replication of treatments.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record says large Daphnia died more; the paper found no significant size difference in survival (0.2-2.0 mm), only a suggestion that larger ones may be more vulnerable. Duration (24 h) was missing.

title: Sensitivity of phytoplankton, zooplankton and macroinvertebrates to hydrogen peroxide treatments of cyanobacterial blooms
scale: 24-h lab tests on 26 taxa (species sensitivity distribution) + two whole-lake H2O2 treatments of Lake Oosterduinse Meer (June and August 2018)
dose: lab graded; lake treatment 1 mean 1.13 mg/L (0.2-2.7 mg/L for 5.5 h), treatment 2 mean 2.19 mg/L (1.7-3.7 mg/L for at least 13 h)
result: Cyanobacteria were most sensitive (24-h EC50 1.39 mg/L for Planktothrix to 3.49 mg/L for Anabaena; green algae ~20x higher, 27.7-74.4 mg/L). The first lake treatment cut cyanobacterial biovolume 85.1% in two days with little non-target effect; the second, stronger and longer, collapsed Dolichospermum by 96.8% but also rotifers by 82.0%.
env_effects: Second lake treatment: 82.0% collapse of rotifers and fewer small cladocerans. Authors' dose classes: <=2 mg/L mild (no non-target effects); 2-4 mg/L harms rotifers and small cladocerans; 4-10 mg/L harms many zooplankton and some macroinvertebrates; 10-100 mg/L suppresses most zooplankton and other eukaryotic phytoplankton.
key_details: 24-h toxicity tests on 3 cyanobacteria, 6 green algae, 8 zooplankton and 9 macroinvertebrate taxa (controls kept >=90% yield or survival) fed a species sensitivity distribution, which was then checked against two treatments of the same Dutch lake. Treatment 1 (mean 1.13 mg/L, gone after 6.5 h; predicted 8 +/- 5% of species affected) cut an Aphanizomenon-dominated bloom by 85.1% of cyanobacterial biovolume in two days without significant effects on most eukaryotic phytoplankton. Treatment 2 (mean 2.19 mg/L, lasting >=13 h; 14 +/- 2% of species affected) collapsed Dolichospermum flos-aquae by 96.8% but also caused an 82.0% rotifer collapse. The SSD predictions matched the lake responses. Only one lake, two treatments, before/after comparison with no control lake.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record listed setting 'lab'; the paper includes two whole-lake field treatments with measured cyanobacterial reductions (85.1%) and a rotifer collapse (82.0%).

title: Combatting cyanobacteria with hydrogen peroxide: a laboratory study on the consequences for phytoplankton community and diversity
scale: bottles at 3 densities
result: Dense water degraded all H2O2 within 24 h except at 50 mg/L (6.3 mg/L left); in diluted water 2.5 mg/L removed the cyanobacterial signal.
env_effects: Greens and diatoms left intact in diluted water.

title: Combined Exposure to Hydrogen Peroxide and LightSelective Effects on Cyanobacteria, Green Algae, and Diatoms
organism: Microcystis aeruginosa PCC 7806, green alga Pseudokirchneriella subcapitata, diatom Navicula seminulum
scale: lab cultures, 27 C, irradiance 0-500 umol/m2/s
dose: H2O2 concentration series (0.6 and 2.5 mg/L for decay tests)
result: EC50 (photosynthetic yield) for Microcystis fell from 6.63 mg/L in the dark to 1.13 at 10, 0.45 at 40 and 0.27 mg/L at 500 umol/m2/s; the green alga (4.05-21.26 mg/L) and diatom (12.19-71.26 mg/L) were roughly 10-60x less sensitive.
env_effects: At 500 umol/m2/s, 2.5 mg/L H2O2 fell to <4% within 3 h (half-life ~0.6 h without algae); Microcystis and Navicula cells degraded it in the dark (half-life 1.6 h). Preadaptation to high light did not reduce sensitivity.
key_details: Short-term (3 h) lab tests of H2O2 toxicity to one cyanobacterium, one green alga and one diatom at five irradiances, with photosynthetic yield (Fv/Fm, PAM fluorometry) as the endpoint and logistic dose-response fits. Light strongly increased toxicity, most for Microcystis (about 20x lower EC50 at 500 umol/m2/s than dark; 5x even at 10 umol/m2/s). Endpoint is photosynthetic inhibition, not cell death or growth. Duplicate measurements for decay tests; high light alone reduced control Fv/Fm by 20-55%.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record said green alga and diatom were 'about 10x less sensitive'; at 500 umol/m2/s they were ~15x (green alga) and ~58x (diatom) less sensitive. Duration (3 h) and the Fv/Fm endpoint were missing.

title: Comparative assessment of algaecide performance on freshwater phytoplankton: Understanding differential sensitivities to frame cyanobacteria management
organism: 12 freshwater strains: cyanobacteria (Synechococcus, Microcystis aeruginosa, Dolichospermum flosaquae), chlorophytes, diatoms, mixotrophs (Cryptomonas, Dinobryon, Prymnesium parvum)
scale: lab; 30 mL cultures in 55 mL tubes, triplicates
result: Mean H2O2 EC50 was 2.18 mg/L for mixotrophs, 4.38 for cyanobacteria, 18.7 for diatoms and 93.26 for chlorophytes (CuSO4 lower for all but chlorophytes); H2O2 is not selective, since mixotrophs and some diatoms were as sensitive as cyanobacteria.
env_effects: Diatoms and mixotrophs nearly as sensitive as cyanobacteria.
key_details: Twelve culture-collection strains in four divisions were exposed in triplicate to six concentrations (0-20 mg/L) of H2O2 or copper sulfate, with photosynthetic yield (Phyto-PAM) giving 48-h EC50s. H2O2 EC50s: Dolichospermum 1.25, Microcystis 4.74, Synechococcus 7.15 mg/L; Cryptomonas 1.80, P. parvum 4.4 mg/L; Navicula 7.8, Cyclotella 11.8 mg/L; chlorophytes 30.14-166.57 mg/L. Copper was more potent than H2O2 in every division except chlorophytes. The authors conclude that H2O2 and CuSO4 give comparable outcomes and that H2O2's selectivity for cyanobacteria is debatable. Monocultures in culture media, not natural communities.
fulltext_discrepancy: Duration (48 h) and the dose range were missing; the ranking in the record matches.

title: Calcium peroxide (CaO2) granules enclosed in fabrics as an alternative H2O2 delivery system to combat Microcystis sp.
scale: bench; 200 mL surface water (Kouris dam) spiked with cultured Microcystis to 8000 RFU; CaO2 granules in 4 fabric types
dose: 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 g/L CaO2 granules (loose or enclosed in fabric)
result: 2.0 g/L CaO2 in fabric types B and C cut phycocyanin fluorescence 87.5-91% and quantum yield 77.8-82.5% by 48 h; lower doses mostly recovered (QY), fabric A barely worked. Granules released up to 12 mg/L H2O2 by 24 h, but residual H2O2 during treatment stayed <0.5 mg/L.
env_effects: Loose granules raised pH above 11; fabric-enclosed systems kept pH at or below ~10 (starting pH 9.5). Toxin release not measured during treatment. No non-target organisms tested.
key_details: Lab bench study, all runs in triplicate at 20 C with continuous light. Artificial bloom: cultured Microcystis added to dam water to Ft 8000 RFU (intracellular MC-RR 4.66 ug/L, MC-YR 1.45 ug/L). Treatments 0-2.0 g/L CaO2 enclosed in fabric types A-C vs no-fabric; control = 0 g/L. Endpoint is fluorescence (Ft) and PSII quantum yield, not cell counts. Only 2.0 g/L (types B, C) and 1 g/L type C gave lasting suppression.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record effect_pct was null; full text gives 87.5-91% Ft reduction at 48 h. Record's pH note ('not in abstract') now filled: loose granules pushed pH >11.

title: Algaecide-Releasing Buoys for Sustained Harmful Algal Bloom Control
scale: lab microcosm: six 1 L beakers of Lake Erie water diluted to 2.0-2.5 ug/L Chl-a (3 with a 20 mL buoy, 3 controls), 10% daily water exchange
dose: small buoy with 1 cm gel loaded with diluted Oximycin P5 (6 g/L H2O2), targeting ~1 mg/L H2O2 in the beaker
result: Buoy release cut Chl-a to 0.07 ug/L after 14 d, about 5% of the control average, with significant reductions at all time points except days 1 and 3; the effect grew over time.
env_effects: 16S rRNA: cyanobacteria fell from ~9% of the bacterial community to 0.24% (day 7) and 1.8% (day 14) vs 1.9% and 5.9% in controls. Biofouling of the buoys needs further work; non-target organisms were not assessed.
key_details: Reusable PVC buoys release a commercial H2O2 algaecide through a polyacrylate hydrogel disk; release followed first-order kinetics set by gel thickness, area and internal concentration, lasting more than a month. The only biological test was a 14-day microcosm: three 1 L beakers with the smallest buoy vs three untreated beakers of Lake Erie water diluted to an early-bloom level (2.0-2.5 ug/L Chl-a), with 10% daily lake-water replacement. Treated Chl-a fell to 0.07 ug/L at day 14, ~5% of the control, significant at all times except days 1 and 3. The starting bloom was deliberately minor (prevention scenario), and medium and large buoys were not tested on algae.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record gave no number; the full text reports Chl-a at ~5% of control after 14 d, but only in 1 L beakers at a very low starting Chl-a (2.0-2.5 ug/L), not a real bloom.

title: The Efficacy of Hydrogen Peroxide in Mitigating Cyanobacterial Blooms and Altering Microbial Communities across Four Lakes in NY, USA | Repeated hydrogen peroxide dosing briefly reduces cyanobacterial blooms and microcystin while increasing fecal bacteria indicators in a eutrophic pond (doi:10.1016/j.jes.2021.11.031)
organism: Cyanobacteria (Planktothrix, Microcystis, Dolichospermum, Cylindrospermopsis, Aphanizomenon) in bloom water from four Long Island lakes/ponds
freshwater_or_marine: freshwater (one brackish site, Georgica Pond 0-20 PSU)
scale: 4 L bottles of field bloom water, incubated outdoors; 11 experiments, 4 water bodies
result: Cyanobacteria fell significantly in 10 of 11 experiments, from on average 85% to 29% of the phytoplankton; cyanobacterial Chl-a was 43-99.8% below controls (e.g. Mill Pond 93-99%, Roth Pond 82%, Lake Agawam 43-52%, one Agawam run not significant).
env_effects: Green algae rose in 6 of 8 experiments (up to 400% above control); heterotrophic bacteria fell 44%; Actinobacteria, Planctomycetes, Verrucomicrobia strongly reduced. Planktothrix most sensitive, Cylindrospermopsis most resistant; Microcystis share of cyanobacteria rose in one run. No fecal-bacteria or whole-pond data in this paper.
key_details: Bottle incubations: each experiment had an unamended control and a 4 mg/L H2O2 treatment, 3 replicate 4 L bottles each, incubated 4-7 d in an outdoor flow-through table. 8 first-round experiments by FluoroProbe; 3 detailed experiments added microscopy, flow cytometry and 16S sequencing. Initial cyanobacterial Chl-a 45-394 ug/L; treatment brought levels below the 25 ug/L NYSDEC threshold only in some runs. Authors conclude H2O2 reduces but does not eliminate cyanobacteria in high-biomass water. The abstract's '4 ug/L' is a typo for 4 mg/L.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record conflated this bottle study with a different Gobler pond-dosing paper: this paper has no whole-pond treatment, no 8 mg/L dose, no 2-week rebound and no fecal-indicator bacteria. Setting should be bottle/mesocosm, not field. effect_pct 82 is a median-ish headline (range 43-99.8%).

title: Hydrogen peroxide treatment promotes chlorophytes over toxic cyanobacteria in a hyper-eutrophic aquaculture pond
scale: lab EC50 tests on 4 cyanobacteria + twelve 1500 L limnocorrals in a 1.5 ha hyper-eutrophic catfish pond (Auburn, AL, May 2017), 3 replicates per dose (one enclosure lost)
result: 6.7 and 20 mg/L gave rapid, sustained cuts in Microcystis and phycocyanin, with day-7 cyanobacterial biovolume 16.4 and 1.5 million um3/mL vs 202.8 million in controls (Table 2); 1.3 mg/L cut Planktothrix but not Microcystis, and chlorophyll a recovered to control levels in all treatments by day 7.
env_effects: Chlorophytes increased. Extracellular microcystin rose 1 day after treatment then fell to control levels by day 7; intracellular microcystin stayed low at 6.7 and 20 mg/L. Zooplankton were significantly suppressed only at 20 mg/L; 6.7 mg/L was similar to control.
key_details: Lab EC50s were ~0.41 mg/L for three filamentous cyanobacteria vs 5.06 mg/L for Microcystis. In the field, twelve 1500 L enclosures of a Planktothrix/Microcystis bloom were dosed once with 0, 1.3, 6.7 or 20 mg/L H2O2 (triplicates; one enclosure damaged) and sampled over 7 days. Phycocyanin stayed very low at 6.7 and 20 mg/L but recovered at 1.3 mg/L; chlorophyll a recovered everywhere by day 7 as chlorophytes replaced cyanobacteria. Day-7 cyanobacterial biovolume at 6.7 mg/L was 91.9% below control (computed from Table 2 means; 99.3% at 20 mg/L). Zooplankton were harmed only at 20 mg/L.
fulltext_discrepancy: The 'field' work was 1500 L enclosures (mesocosm) inside the pond, not a whole-pond treatment; the record gave no reduction figure. effect_pct 91.9 is computed from Table 2, not stated by the authors.

title: Microcystis bloom control using hydrogen peroxide and floating sodium percarbonate algaecide Lake Guard Oxy in Florida
scale: 400 m2 semi-enclosed area below Franklin Lock (S-79), Caloosahatchee River, FL; Lake Guard Oxy spread over 2,023 m2
dose: Liquid: 12 L of 3% H2O2 sprayed, nominal 20 mg/L over top 10 cm (measured peak 73.7 mg/L at 0 min, 4.3 mg/L at 1 h). Lake Guard Oxy (sodium percarbonate): 65 kg on day 2 and day 7 (label max; measured 37.3 mg/L peak at 15 min, 12.6 mg/L at 1 h)
duration: 14 days; 3 treatments (day 0 liquid, days 2 and 7 granules)
result: Short-term: liquid H2O2 vs LGOxy cut cyanobacterial 16S share 79% vs 46%, Chl-a 81% vs 90%, Microcystis colony density 91% vs 97%; effects did not persist beyond ~1 day to a week and the bloom was not eliminated by day 14 (Chl-a still 447 ug/L).
env_effects: H2O2 back to background within 24 h. Alligators, manatees, birds and fish seen in the area with no mortalities in 14 d (visual only). Total microcystin peaked at 35.6 ug/L on day 2; nitrogen-fixation gene expression in diazotrophs rose after LGOxy. Water exchange with the river undid treatments.
key_details: Single-site field trial in a flowing, tidally influenced river; no replicated treatment plots. A reference site outside the treatment area was sampled only on days 0, 1 and 14. H2O2, nutrients, Chl-a, microcystin (ELISA), colony counts, 16S amplicons and transcriptomics measured; triplicate samples from 3 points. Treatment scheme was opportunistic (two organizations working at the same site). Measured H2O2 differed strongly from nominal dose.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record swapped the two Chl-a numbers: liquid H2O2 gave -81% and the percarbonate granules (LGOxy) gave -90%, not the reverse. Doses were given in the paper (nominal 20 mg/L liquid; 65 kg LGOxy per application), not 'not given'.

title: Effects of peroxide-based compounds on growth and toxicity of Microcystis aeruginosa
scale: lab; 200 mL cultures in 300 mL flasks; 5 products (liquid H2O2, CaO2, Lake Guard Oxy, Phycomycin SCP, Oximycin P5)
duration: 9 days (series 1, 150 ug/L Chl-a) and 15 days (series 2 and 3, 300 and 600 ug/L Chl-a)
result: At 150 ug/L Chl-a, Oximycin P5, Phycomycin SCP and liquid H2O2 kept Chl-a undetectable at 1 mg/L, CaO2 and Lake Guard Oxy needed 3 mg/L; at 600 ug/L, CaO2 and Lake Guard Oxy let Chl-a recover at 3 mg/L while the others did not; all products worked at 10 mg/L with no recovery.
env_effects: Extracellular microcystin rose after 1 day in all treatments, then fell below control by day 9. CaO2 raised pH in a dose-dependent way. No non-target organisms tested.
key_details: Three lab series with triplicate flasks per product x dose, at 20 C, 100 umol photons m-2 s-1, 16:8 light. Chl-a and PSII efficiency by PHYTO-PAM; H2O2 by test strips; intra/extracellular microcystins by LC-MS/MS (series 1). Biomass yield analysed by two-way ANOVA (OECD 201 approach). A co-author works for SePRO, which makes two of the tested products.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record duration 'Not reported' -> 9 and 15 days. Record omitted that Chl-a was driven to zero (effective 100%) at >=3 mg/L for most products, and the transient extracellular-toxin rise.
